comment.value:
Overall
=====
This work surfaces an important gap in the visual reasoning abilities of sota VLLMs and scores are mostly positive after rebuttal and discussion (5, 4, 4, 5). I recommend the acceptance of this work as poster.

Summary
=======
The authors propose a new VQA benchmark that consists of asking models what objects in common across multiple images that are not available in existing data sources. Remarkably, commercial models such as GPT4 not only achieve low performance (35% on the easy version and 1% on the complex version) but also hallucinate objects.

Strengths
=======
* Novel and valuable benchmark
* High-quality dataset construction: Combines 45% real-world images (manually captured by authors, ensuring no training data contamination) with 55% synthetic images (Unreal Engine), providing guaranteed ground truth and scalable difficulty levels with up to 16 objects per scene.
* Extensive evaluation and analysis: Evaluates 13 models across 5 families with thorough analysis of perception vs. reasoning performance, hallucination rates (up to 80%), object complexity effects, and insights into multi-image training benefits, providing clear evidence of current model limitations.

Weaknesses
=========
The authors did a good job addressing the following concerns in the rebuttal:

* Limited prompting evaluation and potential bias: Only one prompting method was tested, which could significantly impact results.
  * Reviewer 4rcr: "There's only one potential prompting method evaluated (L156), and I'm a bit concerned that the format might be directly related to the performance of the models"
  * Reviewer ibjw: "The evaluation does neither ablate the choice of prompt (one single prompt) nor the decoding strategy (greedy). Both may severely influence the performance"
* Insufficient evaluation of reasoning-capable models: The paper concludes models struggle with reasoning but doesn't test models specifically designed for reasoning tasks.
  * Reviewer jTB8: "Considering the paper made a conclusion that existing models perform not well when reasoning across scenes, more capable reasoning models are suggested to be included to enrich this paper. This could include QVQ-72B"
  * Reviewer ibjw: "While the paper benchmarks multiple frontier models, the low accuracy may not be that surprising if these models have not seen similar tasks during training. It would be useful to additionally benchmark models [1,2] that have been specifically trained to detect commonalities"
* Poor writing quality and missing key details: The paper lacks clear task definitions and important methodological details.
  * Reviewer DN7v: "The paper is poor in writing: 1.1. I can not find the task definition throughout the paper, just guessing it from Figure 1" and "It is not documented how the candidate object set is created"
  * Reviewer ibjw: "It would be useful to add a human baseline with unbiased participants"
* Lack of specialized model evaluation: the authors resolved this in the rebuttal "new QvQ-72B reasoning model results (thanks to reviewer jTB8) showing this specialized model does not saturate the benchmark (achieving only 12% accuracy) and new multi versus single-image evaluations across 13 leading multimodal models."

author_final_remarks.value:
Thank all the reviewers for their thoughtful suggestions. We are thrilled all reviewers found merit in 

* **Common-O’s motivation**: “tackles a simple, unique, and interesting problem: can models reason about joint object existence across multiple images?” (review 4rcr)  and that “identifying objects across scenes is a valuable task and may be the foundation ability for other tasks.” (reviewer DN7v).   
* **Common-O’s quality and scale**: Common-O “ is of very high quality containing 10.5k samples” (reviewer ibjw), “the dataset is fairly large”  (reviewer 4rcr), and noting “scale and the performance of existing models, as compared to existing multi-image benchmarks.” (reviewer  jTB8)   
* **Common-O’s presentation**: noting "well written and clearly illustrated.” (reviewer ibjw) and “the presentation, including tables and figures, along with the writings, are overall clear to me” (reviewer jTB8).

We’re grateful for all the feedback and engagement from reviewers. Based on their feedback, we’ve made considerable improvements to our submission:

* **Confirming the robustness of our findings:**  
  * New prompt variations and temperature ablations: we evaluate 3 prompt variations to confirm the robustness of our findings across range of temperatures from 0 to 1.
  * Statistical analysis of error bars (suggested by reviewer ibjw and 4rcr): bootstrapping 1000 iterations showing small standard errors (\<1%) (see table)  
* **Controls to better understand drivers of performance**: differences in the number of objects in scenes or backgrounds are not the primary drivers of what makes Common-O challenging (see new statistical analysis and table).  
* **Extending Common-O**:  
  * Additional models: new QvQ-72B reasoning model results (thanks to reviewer jTB8) showing this specialized model does not saturate the benchmark (achieving only 12% accuracy) and new multi versus single-image evaluations across 13 leading multimodal models.  
  * Extending Common-O to image triplets (based on reviewer DN7v’s suggestion): we found this setting to be even more challenging across 10 leading models.

In all, we believe Common-O establishes a valuable new benchmark to measure reasoning across scenes for multimodal models—a challenging new milestone for driving progress in multimodal research. Thank you to the reviewers and AC for your service to the community and for carefully considering our work.

Based on your suggestion, we additionally ran new ablations for temperature to better understand the effect of temperature on the overall performance. We report the performance on Common-O across various temperature values and note our originally reported performance is consistently among the highest performing, thereby confirming the robustness of our conclusions to the choice of temperature. I thank the authors for their rebuttal, which addresses many of my comments. Here are a few more comments/questions from my side:

> We appreciate the suggestion to benchmark these specialized models. Given the short-time frame of the rebuttal, we unfortunately were not able to include these specific models. We however, were able to run an additional analysis using QvQ-72B, a frontier multimodal model explicitly advertised as a model capable of visual reasoning. We find even QvQ still struggles to reason across scenes, achieving only 12% on Common-O. Finally, by releasing our benchmark, we also encourage the community to extend our evaluations to a broader set of frontier and specialized models.

I appreciate the addition of QvQ-72B, but this model is also not explicitly trained/finetuned for this task. However, while it would be interesting to see the performance of specialized models, I do not see this as a major weakness. It might be useful to reference these papers in the background and or conclusion for future readers.

> We agree frontier models can be sensitive to choice of prompt. In addition to exploring both alphabetized multiple choice (see Section 3.2) and explicit object enumeration which we explored earlier in our work (yielding comparable results), based on your feedback we ran additional evaluations on Llama 4 using two new prompt reformulations. We find these results of ~3% performance difference confirm that even across prompt variations frontier models struggle with low performance on Common-O.

Where can I find these results? And was the sampling itself ablated? For some of these models, a non-zero temperature is recommended for optimal results on benchmarks.

rebuttal.value:
We would like to thank the reviewer for highlighting the importance of our contribution and for insightful suggestions to improve our work, which we address in turn below.

**Additional frontier models**
We appreciate the suggestion to benchmark these specialized models. Given the short-time frame of the rebuttal, we unfortunately were not able to include these specific models. We however, were able to run an additional analysis using QvQ-72B, a frontier multimodal model explicitly advertised as a model capable of visual reasoning. We find even QvQ still struggles to reason across scenes, achieving only 12% on Common-O. Finally, by releasing our benchmark, we also encourage the community to extend our evaluations to a broader set of frontier and specialized models.

**Creation of candidate object sets**
This is a good point. We decided to focus on common everyday objects that can be found in an office or household that can be easily classified by multimodal models. We confirm multimodal models were able to recognize the objects in our dataset. To collect the images photographers followed the guidelines provided in Supplementary Appendix B. We will be sure to expand our discussion of these choices in our revised submission.

**Choice of prompt + decoding strategy**

We agree frontier models can be sensitive to choice of prompt. Thank you for your detailed review and feedback! We address your questions below.

1. **Performance as the number of objects in a scene increases.**

This is a great point. We agree of course, recognition even for humans, increases in difficulty as the number of objects in a scene grows. While the increasing difficulty in perception as the number of objects grows is certainly a contributing factor, it’s the combination of perception and reasoning across scenes that makes our benchmark difficult. We’d like to clarify that only Common-O-Complex has N=16 objects, while the main Common-O benchmark includes a maximum of only 7 objects per scene.

We confirm the performance in Common-O is not primarily driven by the difficulty of the recognition task as the number of objects per scene grows. To do so, we run an additional analysis where we keep the number of objects per scene fixed and compare model performance on the Common-O multi-image reasoning versus single image recognition task. 

We find even when the same number of objects per scene is represented in single image versus multi-image Common-O, there is a significant difference in performance suggesting although models excel at single image perception, comparing objects in common across scenes remains a challenge:

| 4                         | 0.8296                  | 0.2030                       |
| 5                         | 0.8062                  | 0.1401                       |
| 6                         | 0.8073                  | 0.0845                       |
| 7                         | 0.8104                  | 0.1111                       |

We believe a future milestone for advancing multimodal vision models is to progress on tasks that require both perception and reasoning. We design both Common-O and Common-O-Complex such that both good perception and reasoning across scenes is necessary to perform well on the task. We’ll be sure to include this new analysis in our camera ready and thank you for the suggestion.

2. **Different prompting methods**

We agree frontier models can certainly be brittle. In addition to exploring both alphabetized multiple choice (see Section 3.2) and explicit object enumeration which we explored earlier in our work (yielding comparable results), based on your feedback we ran additional evaluations using two new prompt reformulations. Thank you for your careful review of our work and thoughtful feedback. We’re glad you found our new benchmark reveals a well motivated deficiency of existing models to reason across scenes. We’re glad you found the presentation clear, the analysis between perception and reasoning sufficient, and noted the scale of our dataset. We thank you for the thoughtful suggestions and address each below.

**Additional reasoning models:** thank you for the suggestion. Based on your feedback, we ran additional evaluations using QVQ-72B, a leading multimodal model. We found QVQ-72B achieved only 12% accuracy on Common-O suggesting improved visual mathematical reasoning may not be sufficient for reasoning about common objects across scenes. We will include results for additional models including MM-Eureka in the camera ready.

**Correlation between gains on synthetic and real:** we thank you for raising this important point. We include synthetic images, not only for scale, but also because we were able to use a wider range of backgrounds and relative object sizes that are less easy to achieve when taking our own images (e.g. the plane and cast iron skillet are the same size on the bottom right in Figure 2). 

Thanks to your suggestion, we ran an additional analysis comparing the performance gains on synthetic versus real subsets of Common-O. We compare the performance of all 13 models evaluated across the synthetic and real partitions of Common-O. To evaluate whether gains on synthetic transfer to real images in Common-O we compute Pearson’s correlation coefficient. We find a high Pearson’s correlation of 0.792 suggesting gains on synthetic are correlated with gains on real images (and vice versa). We will be sure to include this additional analysis in the camera-ready version of our work.

**Complexity of background:** This is another great point. We intentionally selected simple backgrounds to avoid variation in backgrounds from affecting model performance. Based on your feedback, we ran an additional control to assess whether backgrounds have a significant effect on perception performance. We first sample 18k images with background labels. We then compare perception performance across backgrounds using a t-test. We find there is no statistically significant evidence the performance differs from the mean across backgrounds (t-statistic 0.0027, pvalue=0.99) suggesting backgrounds do not significantly alter perception performance.

**Detailed statistics:** Good suggestion! We have 129 objects in Common-O. You’ll also find details on the dataset statistics in the data card available in the supplementary material. Thanks to your suggestion, we additionally explore the average size of each object using segmentations from SAM. We find each object ranges from 2-22% of the image size.
We’ll also be sure to release meta-data associated with samples in our camera-ready to make it as easy as possible for the community to conduct further analysis. 

**Typo:** Thanks! We’ve fixed the typo in the main paper.

We believe the additional reasoning model evaluation, correlation analysis between synthetic & real, suggested inclusion of dataset statistics, as well as the additional background complexity control based on your feedback have improved the quality of our submission. We thank you once again for this feedback and hope you consider these new results in your final score. We remain available for any further discussion.

summary.value: This paper introduces Common-O Bench, a benchmarks containing 10.5K examples asking if VLMs can perform multi-image commonality reasoning, and Common-O Complex, an expanded version containing 12.5K examples. Each sample consists of two images a scene containing up to 16 objects (from potentially different views), and asks, given a set of "Choices" which objects within the "Choices" are present in both images. Images can be either synthetic (generated with Unreal Engine, 55%) or real (taken by the authors, 45%). The paper evaluates 5 families of models (13 models), and shows that while models are capable of recognizing objects (achieving ~80% accuracy), they are incapable of reasoning jointly about the objects, and achieve accuracies of less than 40% in simple tasks, and <1% on complex tasks. Models also have high rates of hallucination, with hallucinations occurring in as many as 80% of samples.

strengths_contributions.value:
- The paper tackles a simple, unique, and interesting problem: can models reason about joint object existence across multiple images? And does this lead to large rates of hallucination? 
- The dataset is fairly large, and is composed of a mixture of real and synthetic images. For the real images, there is guaranteed to be no overlap with existing training data, as the images are not sourced from online references.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- The paper doesn't really acknowledge the baseline combinatorics for N=16 objects. If models have even 80% recognition accuracy, it is unlikely that a model with that recognition accuracy can achieve strong no-hallucination performance just due to simple recognition errors. It would be good to discuss some of the simple combinatorics when discussing the recognition vs. reasoning performance.
- There's only one potential prompting method evaluated (L156), and I'm a bit concerned that the format might be directly related to the performance of the models, particularly the requirement that the model produce all of the samples in one generation pass. It would be good to perform a couple of prompting ablations, such as looking at "Is the X present in both scenes?" which could help disambiguate prompting error/variance from actual reasoning performance. Similarly, work has shown that multiple choice answer order can impact performance, and it would be good to see if this is the case for this dataset as well. 
- The analysis primarily focuses on overall accuracy and hallucination rates, but does not really look deeply into why models hallucinate or what kinds of object similarities or scene configurations cause the biggest problems. It would be helpful from a long-term design perspective to have some of this information, or a more detailed qualitative error analysis. 
- There's no real statistical analysis in the benchmark tables, and it would be good to at least include some idea of variance (perhaps standard error around the mean for bootstrapped samples) for each of the experiments.

Related work:
- This task is somewhat similar to the multimodal task in [1], which asks models to reason across large numbers of images, for simple presence based existence.


[1] Wu, Tsung-Han, et al. "Visual Haystacks: A Vision-Centric Needle-In-A-Haystack Benchmark." The Thirteenth International Conference on Learning Representations.

summary.value: This paper proposed a new multi-image dataset, Common-O, characterized by its large scale (22k) and complexity. By asking existing models about simple cognitive question "what is the common objects across images?", the proposed benchmark reveals the deficiency of existing models on reasoning across scenes, where even best-performing models only achieve 35% (1% on its "complex" subset). The paper carefully analyses the behaviors of these models, providing insights for reasoning across images.

strengths_contributions.value:
+ Motivation. The overall motivation for collecting this data is clear and straightforward to me.
+ Dataset. The dataset itself has enough contributions considering its scale and the performance of existing models, as compared to existing multi-image benchmarks.
+ Analysis. Authors have done sufficient analyses over the relation between perception and reasoning, performance changes with respect to scene complexity (num. of objects), and how reasoning, multi-image training, model scale affects model behaviors on Common-o.
+ Presentation. The presentation, including tables and figures, along with the writings, are overall clear to me.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
+ Evaluation of Reasoning Models and Approaches. I notice that authors have included reasoning cases in Figure 6a, including DeepSeekVL2 and LlamaV-o1. Considering the paper made a conclusion that existing models perform not well when reasoning across scenes, more capable reasoning models are suggested to be included to enrich this paper. This could include QVQ-72B, for example, and the recent models that involves RL post-training where reasoning is somewhat incentivized, such as MM-Eureka.
+ Correlation of performance between synthetic and real. Authors have analysed the individual contributions from synthetic and real subsets from Common-o. What is more, it is suggested that authors present the correlations between synthetic and real subsets. Will performance gains on synthetic subsets positively correlate to those on real subsets?
+ Complexity of background. The complexity of foreground is fully discussed, but the background appears easy for LVLMs.
+ Lack of Detailed Statistics. The authors are suggested to include more details about the evaluated objects, including sizes, numbers of objects, indicating diverse difficulty levels.

summary.value: This paper introduces "Common-O", a benchmark probing multimodal LLM abilities to spot a set of common objects over two different scenes. The benchmark consists of 10.5k samples with 45% of them being manually taken by the authors and the remaining 3D rendered. The benchmark is split into two sets by hardness: "Common-O Bench" contains samples with at most 7 objects, and "Common-O Complex" contains samples with 8-16 objects per scene. The study evaluates multiple closed and open-source models, showing that even SOTA models fail to identify commonalities over two scenes (< 35% on Bench, < 1% on Complex) and models often hallucinate while doing so. The authors also identify a weak-moderate correlation between intra-scene object similarity and accuracy.

strengths_contributions.value:
- Common-O probes visual perception and reasoning through the lens of common objects in two scenes. It is a much more structured approach than previous work.
- The proposed benchmark is of very high quality containing 10.5k samples mixing both human annotated real-world photos and synthetic renditions.
- The benchmark has the opportunity to scale in hardness, as the authors demonstrated that the synthetic subset is ever harder than real-world data due to additional invariances that can be modeled (e.g., size of objects).
- SOTA models perform poorly on this dataset, not even reaching 1% of accuracy on the complex subset, demonstrating the hardness of this benchmark.
- The paper is well written and clearly illustrated.
- The study measures accuracy and hallucination and gives additional insights beyond the evaluation itself (challenges due to similar objects, real vs synthetic, scaling effects etc.)

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- While the paper benchmarks multiple frontier models, the low accuracy may not be that surprising if these models have not seen similar tasks during training. It would be useful to additionally benchmark models [1,2] that have been specifically trained to detect commonalities or differences.  
- It is not documented how the candidate object set is created. 
- The evaluation does neither ablate the choice of prompt (one single prompt) nor the decoding strategy (greedy). Both may severely influence the performance. It would be great to test a few alternative prompts and to see if temperature scaling+sampling has a strong influence on the results.
- It would be useful to add a human baseline with unbiased participants (i.e., not the authors). This would help to solidify the contextualization of the results better, although one may argue that the relatively high inter-rater accuracy (84%) is sufficient. 
- Figure 6b,c should be updated to show error bars.

Minor issues:
- L48 missing whitespace before "Common"
- The ref in L237 is wrong and should point to Figure 6 (?)
- L255: "Limitations" -> "Limitations."

[1] Li et al, "MIMIC-IT: Multi-Modal In-Context Instruction Tuning", Preprint, 2023.
[2] Lin et al., "Comparison visual instruction tuning", CVPR-W, 2025 (preprint since 2024).

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: The dataset construction and evaluation format are well described in the paper. The dataset is hosted on Kaggle.

summary.value: This paper introduces a new task to identify the common objects existing in a paired of images. By benchmarking existing models, the paper finds that while models can handle the problem with single-image problems, they struggle across multi-image scenarios. Equipping the model with long CoT thinking ability may not improve the performance while training with multi images may work.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. Identifying objects across scenes is a valuable task and may be the foundation ability for other tasks.
2. The paper propose to evaluate models with an enlightening baseline, ie single image evaluation, highlighting the problem under the multi-image scenario.
3. The proposed task can be synthesized in an efficient way, possibly using for training.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The paper is poor in writing:

1.1. I can not find the task definition throughout the paper, just guessing it from Figure 1.

1.2. In the introduction, authors should clarify why the new task is valuable or the necessity for MLLMs to obtain this ability. Saturated performance on other visual perception tasks is not the reason for introducing this new benchmark.

1.3. Authors should provide the exact numbers in the main result table (Figure 3) so that the following works can make accurate comparisons.

2. I think authors should provide more analysis on why models perform well on single-image scenarios while struggling with multi-image inputs. This may shed light on possible improvement directions for future works.

3. Why is this task a reasoning task? As shown in Figure 6(a), reasoning with long CoT may not improve the performance. What ability is needed to tackle this problem?

4. As shown in the paper, models trained on multi-image inputs show improved ability. Authors can synthesize more samples and finetune one model to see whether this is a simple problem that can be tackled by naive finetuning.

5. The task can be further extended to multi-image (more than 2) and multi-background (beyond multi-views of the single background).

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

final_justification.value:
The paper comes up with a good idea of reasoning across scenes. During rebuttal, authors supplement many crucial experiments and analysis, all of which should be included in the final version of the manuscript. After reading the rebuttal and comments from other reviewers, I update my final score as  Borderline accept.

Similar to Reviewer ibjw, evaluating specialized models or providing simple finetuning results can make the analysis more insightful. Hoping authors can update the results when more time is available.

title.value: What’s in Common? Multimodal Models Hallucinate When Reasoning Across Scenes

TLDR.value: we release a cognitively-inspired benchmark for reasoning across scenes that reveals hallucination is an open challenge for multimodal models

abstract.value: Multimodal language models possess a remarkable ability to handle an open-vocabulary worth of objects. Yet the best models still suffer from hallucinations when reasoning about scenes in the real world, revealing a gap between their seemingly strong performance on existing perception benchmarks that are saturating and their reasoning in the real world. To address this gap, we build a novel benchmark of in-the-wild scenes that we call Common-O Bench with more than 10.5k examples using exclusively new images not found in web training data to avoid contamination, Common-O goes beyond just perception, inspired by cognitive tests for humans, to probe reasoning across scenes by asking ``what’s in common?''. We evaluate leading multimodal language models, including models specifically trained to reason. We find that perceiving objects in single images is easy for most models, yet reasoning across scenes is very challenging even for the best models, including reasoning models. Despite saturating many leaderboards focusing on perception, the best performing model only achieves 35\% on Common-O Bench---and on Common-O Complex, consisting of more complex scenes, the best model achieves only 1\%. Curiously, we find models are more prone to hallucinate when similar objects are present in the scene, suggesting models may be relying on object co-occurrence seen during training. Among the models we evaluated, we found scale can provide modest improvements while models explicitly trained with multi-image inputs show bigger improvements, suggesting scaled multi-image training may offer promise. We make our benchmark publicly available to spur research into the challenge of hallucination when reasoning across scenes.
